newsitem.title: JAPAN: Lee Kuan Yew blasts Hong Kong governor's reforms.
newsitem.headline: Lee Kuan Yew blasts Hong Kong governor's reforms.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa would lose China's trust if he kept the democratic reforms introduced by the colony's last British governor, Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew said on Friday.

"(Tung) has been criticised for not defending and preserving Governor (Chris) Patten's democratic initiatives. But were he to do so, he would totally lose China's confidence," Lee said in a lecture in Tokyo.

While rolling back Patten's reforms, Tung, who becomes Hong Kong's chief executive on July 1, can maintain the civil and economic liberties that Hong Kong had enjoyed before the changes pushed through by the territory's last British governor.

"He can protect and maintain the freedoms and liberties which Hong Kong enjoyed before Governor Patten attempted to enlarge them, provided this is to preserve Hong Kong's system, and not to change the system in Guangdong province, or worse, the PRC," Lee said.

Lee, one of Asia's foremost exponents of firm government rule, pointedly excluded the Patten democratic reforms from what he listed as Britain's positive legacy in Hong Kong: sound administration and legal framework and financial discipline.
"Patten's political agenda has provided a stick for foreign lobby groups to beat China with," Lee said in a seminar on Hong Kong's future after the July 1 handover to China.

Beijing has already selected a provisional legislature to replace Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council on July 1 and has unveiled plans to cut back civil and political liberties when it reabsorbs Hong Kong as a special administrative region.

In response to criticism in Hong Kong and abroad, Tung on Thursday announced a partial retreat from curbs on rights, narrowing a ban on foreign political funding and moderating previously planned limits on the right to protest.

Singapore, a former British colony that Lee led to independence in the early 1960s and then ruled as prime minister until 1990, allows widespread economic freedoms but keeps tight controls on political activity and the media.
